To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the saccadic response speed of human subjects can be explained by a model of spatial attention that is based on a precision-dependent gain control of sensory input.
saccadic response speed is best explained by a model of Bayesian belief updates in which the precision of beliefs about target location determines the speed of the saccadic response.

the speed with which a subject responds to a target stimulus is a measure of the precision with which the subject has updated his belief about the location of that target, and that the speed of responding is determined by the precision of that belief.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question how probabilistic information in the environment is integrated into the brain's internal models of the world and how this process is reflected in behavior.
how the brain adapts its behavior in a changing world.
the neural mechanisms underlying the ability of the brain to infer and adapt to the environment's statistical regularities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the brain's ability to adapt to the environment's statistical regularities, and thereby optimize behavior accordingly, may rely on precision-dependent modulation of the gain of neural responses.
the present results are consistent with the hypothesis that spatial attention is modulated by precision-dependent gain control.
the results of the current study are in line with a Bayesian account of attentional orienting.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brain's ability to infer the statistical structure of the environment and adapt behavior accordingly is a key feature of its computational function.
the brain's ability to infer the environment's statistical properties and adapt behavior accordingly can be studied in a simple form of spatial attentional orientating.
spatial attention is a function of precision.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain can be modeled as a Bayesian inference machine, and that such a model can be tested with psychophysical experiments.
Bayesian inference can be directly observed in the behavior of subjects in a simple experimental task.
the brain can use the precision of its beliefs to adapt behavior to a changing statistical environment, and that this precision-dependent gain modulation is reflected in saccade reaction times.
